[h1] Hacknet [/h1]

[b] Introduction [/b]

Hacknet is by far the best game that i have ever played, i'll tell you why. 
To describe it the most simple it is a text based adventure however in reality it is much more then that.
The story starts of rather cliche with a "if you are reading this i am already dead" though the writer of said story has got a lot more planned. 

The basic premise behind Hacknet is as the name suggests "Hacking" though its not your typical CSI mash the buttons fast enough to blow up the CIA sort of hacking. If you aren't familiar with it most hacking is done by exe's and lines of code not a test for how fast you can type the word flamingo. 

Most of the commands in hacknet are actually based of UNIX a type of coding language and common PC ports such as SMPT, which is for mail as an example. 

[b] story [/b]

The game revolves around the story of you, the player, getting hold of some software known as "Hacknet" basically a UI (User-interface) to easily conduct all your hacking adventures. This program also has a powerful tool known as "porthack" that can be used to eventually break into someone else's computer, this program is quite important later in the story. In the beggining of the game you are greeted by "Bit" or at least his messages that he has left behind. Through an E-Mail system, that is primarly used for attaining new missions, he explains some basics to you. 

[b] gameplay [/b]

The thing in Hacknet you are going to spend the most time doing is hacking, this is one by using commands to launch programs that will open up ports on a computer, then once they are all open you can use the aformentioned "Porthack" to finnaly break into the computer, After wich you have to erase your activity of being there so that someone cannot find out if you were there. As the game progresses these sequences become harder for example: adding timers, that when run out will shut down your virtual hacknet computer. a firewall that you have to "analyze" to unlock its password in order to use the "porthack" program. and a proxy that you have to disable with programs run on computer you have already hacked, if this proxy is active you cannot use any of the commands needed for opening up ports. 

As the story progresses you find new and interesting ports which you may not have a solution to at first but you will find clever tricks to get around problems you cannot solve by hacking related servers, scanning them for phones and pulling e-mail data out of those to figure out how to solve whatever "puzzle" is stopping you from progressing. Often the characters in the game will give sublte hints via the e-mail system in updates they give after you have completed certain tasks that they asked you to do. 

[b] The "feel" [/b]

for a text based game it has probably the most tense ending that i have played out of all games ever which really made me realize how good it was. 

The characters you meet feel real and "exploration" is very rewarding and can often get you programs or other secret questlines you might have never uncovered otherwise.

I have played this game about 6 times now and i still cannot get enough of it, even now with an added feature to create your complete own storyline inside the game just continues to amaze me. 

[b] flaws [/b]

The only problem i have with it is that at very certain moments the Tab key that auto completes names and commands doesnt completely work and you have to type out and remember a few long words but that's mostly fine. Personally i dont know anything about programming at all yet i was really able to enjoy this game.

[b] conclusion [/b]

For its not massive price tag this is an excellent game that i urge anyone that has a keyboard to play, all in all excellent story and a great atmosphere. a solid 9.5

When I was younger, I used to use IRC often and would spend my days rummaging through people's shared folders to download bits and bobs. This game reminded me a lot of that. It was a lot of fun using "programs" to stickybeak into private computer systems in the game to achieve various objectives. From a gameplay point of view, it's not terribly complex - once you've learnt the few commands there is to know, you'll basically be using them repeatedly to achieve objectives. Some parts of the game requires some fast typing. Most of the game is you paying attention to files in various systems and gleaning the necessary information to move onto the next step. There are some puzzle elements that will require you to pay attention to the information you've gathered.

The game's a little light on the story but it's not bad. I spent most of it on side missions/contracts. I'll be replaying to complete the ones I've missed. You can probably finish the game completely in about 8 hours if you're diligent, I'll likely complete it in about 10-11 hours. 

Anyway, I had a lot of fun playing this game, and definitely recommend it to those who like puzzles, rummaging for info, and pretending to hack into computers!

I enjoyed this title, for what little I played of it. A fun little hacking simulator. The story isn't amazing, and there are a few details in this game that I usually think don't make for great gaming experiences. One of those things is one off opportunities to follow a side story that completely disappear if you don't do exactly what you're supposed to, across multiple steps. I suppose you could argue those are good for replayability, but if those opportunities are 5 hours into the game, I doubt you'll want to experiment to figure out the correct path, fail, and start over with another 5 hours to try again. That kind of trial-and-error gameplay has been ditched for decades at this point, because it's not fun. I suppose you could just use a guide if you are a completionist but don't want to spend time replaying the same stuff over and over.

In addition, the game has a number of moments where you are wondering where to go next, with no obvious options. Sometimes it's a bug that the story isn't moving, and sometimes you just have no idea what next step advances the story. Another moment for a guide.

Regardless of those minor quibbles, the game is worth $10 for the 10 hours I put into it. I have no desire to return at this point, and I got 50% of the way through, but I will likely pick it back up again when I'm home sick for a little time waster.

Steam needs to update the rating system. This thumbs up/down is just too simplistic. While I do recommend the game for those who never played a hack "sim" before, I get the feeling that some people who are used to Uplink will be disappointed.

Uplink is the only game like this one I've played, and Hacknet is obviously inspired by it, so this is basically a comparison between the 2.

If you played Uplink this will be a walk in the park. Aside from visuals, there's nothing here that Uplink didn't do better back in 2001. With the excepton of a couple of moments, all missions are exactly the same all the way through, so it gets repetitive quite fast. 

There's no sense of danger or urgency Uplink gives you. Nobody will come after you, there's no police, companies you hack won't give a shit. Despite of what the game tells you right at the beggining, there's no need to cover your tracks. In Uplink, everytime you hack into a system it's a race against time. In Hacknet there's nothing like it. Once you block a trace you can spend as much time as you want in any system.

There's no rig upgrades, no rewards, nothing like it. You just complete the mission, get a "thank you" email and move on to the next.  

Both games have a story, but Uplink is more of a sandbox. After you get the hang of it you can do whatever you want and follow the story whenever you want. Hacknet, on the other hand, is pretty linear. That's a big dissapointment, specially after a great "wtf do I do now" moment right in the beggining. After that, you get the feeling you're never safe, but unfortunately nothing like that ever happens again. Storywise, Uplink is way more interesting, while Hacknet is cliche and way too simplistic.

That's the main problem with this game. It's way too easy. Uplink is infuriating unforgiven to the player. Once you start to mess with big companies, one small screw up means game over. Add that to the fact that the game is pretty much a roguelike, so it's not like you can go back to a previous save, you have to start all over again. In Hacknet, you don't need to worry about that. Like I said before, there's no need to clean after you. If you get caught, all you need to do is change your ip adress.

Anyway, if you never played a hacking "sim" before, this might be a good place to start. Like Uplink, It's really easy to get into, you don't need to now anything about code to play both games, and they give you a good sense of immersion.   

Hacknet has a good concept, but is way too simple for those looking for a challenge. I hope the "Labyrinths" expansion adds more substance to the game.

As far as unique gaming experiences go (and let's be honest, they're hard to find some days), Hacknet delivers spectacularly. Not your traditional game in any way, Hacknet lets you live out that "1337 hax0r" fantasy most techies have felt at some point in their lives. The game can be a little repetitive at times, and the final third of the game is where it really shines, but the experience as a whole is a lot of fun and prompts you to think in some unexpected ways. No previous command line experience is truly required thanks to the visual interface, but you might understand the workflow a little better if you've worked with a terminal before. Regardless of your experience, definitely give Hacknet a go; it's worth your time.
